name: Fanagalo
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Bold, John D. (1968) Fanagalo: phrase-book, grammar and dictionary (one of 9 grammars in Glottolog, 1888-1996); none online; Wikipedia phonology section has no stress statement

new_statements.quote: Stress. In Fanagalo the stress, or accentuation, usually falls on the penultimte [sic; 1953 ed.: penultimate] syllable of the word. Here is an example, with the accentuated syllables in bold type: Washa masandla gawena (wash your hands). By the same token the final syllable in Fanagalo words, particularly those which have an Nguni origin, is usually weak and unaccentuated. [p. 4] ... M or N at the beginning of a word, if followed by a consonant, are accorded full value as a syllable. In the original Nguni they were spelt UM, IM or IN, and should be given just as much stress. [p. 4] — Corroboration, Lloyd n.d. [c.1913] p. 4: 'ACCENTUATION. The Accent falls on the last syllable but one.'
new_statements.citation: Bold, J. D. 1990. Fanagalo: Phrase-Book, Grammar, Dictionary. 15th revised edition (first published by CNA 1951). Pretoria: J. L. van Schaik. (Same wording in Bold 1953, Dictionary and Phrase-Book of Fanagalo (Kitchen Kafir), 2nd ed., Central News Agency, p. 9.)

By the same token the final syllable in Fanagalo words, particularly those which have an Nguni origin, is usually weak and unaccentua…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word (as in the Nguni lexifier); the final syllable, especially in Zulu/Nguni-derived words, is weak and unstressed. Word-initial syllabic nasals (mlungu, nkosi < umlungu, inkosi) count as full syllables for this purpose. Lloyd's early Kitchen-Kafir grammar gives the same rule ('last syllable but one'). APiCS (Mesthrie & Surek-Clark 2013) independently reports Nguni-style penultimate vowel lengthening and no lexical tone apart from a few deictic pairs.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Bold hedges with 'usually'; no specific exceptions listed. Bold's example 'Washa masandla gawena' shows penultimate stress on each word of a phrase (bold type in original: Washa, masandla, gawena). APiCS notes tonal contrast only on deictics lò/ló, làpha/lápha.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level ('the penultimate syllable of the word'); the example is a three-word phrase with each word stressed on its penult. Bold's book is a practical phrase-book/grammar by a non-linguist, aimed at employers; Lloyd's is a c.1913 popular booklet; neither is instrumental or a professional phonological description, hence medium confidence despite full agreement across three independent-era sources.
new_statements.identity_note: Bold's phrase-book (title page 1953: 'as spoken in the Union of South Africa, the Rhodesias, Portuguese East Africa, Nyasaland, Belgian Congo, etc.') describes the general Zulu-lexified pidgin = fana1235 proper, not a specific mine or farm register; Lloyd's booklet describes the same pidgin under its older name 'Kitchen-Kafir' (Johannesburg/Kimberley, early 20th c.). Glottolog dialects Chilapalapa [chil1261] (Zimbabwe/Zambia) and Cikabanga [cika1238] are covered by Bold's scope but not separately described for stress. APiCS chapter 61 (Mesthrie & Surek-Clark) covers Mine and Farm Fanakalo together.

sources.note: Section 4 Phonology does not use the word stress; it states 'Penultimate vowels – as in Nguni – are typically lengthened: thus [bu:ga] "see" versus [bugi:le] "saw". Tonal distinctions are not made, apart from the deictics: lò "this" versus ló "that" (versus lo "the"); làpha "here", lápha "there"'. Vowel length not phonemic. (html saved locally as well.)
